description: We are a passionate and driven team participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge, specializing in AI, programming, and innovative problem-solving. We are looking for creative and dedicated team members (developers, UI/UX designers, and data enthusiasts) who are excited to build impactful solutions using NASA's open data. Let's create something amazing together
summary: On a long mission to Mars a message to Earth takes up to about 20 minutes each way, so the crew is the first line of care. Ordinary health apps use one fixed "normal range" for everybody. AstroPulse instead learns each astronaut's own normal from their first week, flags a steady drift while the colors are still green, explains it through NASA's five hazards of spaceflight, and tells the crew what to do now while showing how long Earth needs to answer. A phone-camera pulse measurement needs no extra hardware.
details:
WHAT IT DOES. AstroPulse is a web app with a crew view and a ground-control view. Every health indicator (heart rate, oxygen, skin temperature, blood pressure, blood sugar, sleep, mood) has a color, a plain-language explanation tied to NASA's five hazards of spaceflight, and a decision screen with an Earth-delay counter (Station, Moon, Mars). Each person is compared with their own first week: a sustained drift (4 days, 2 standard deviations or more) is flagged even while fixed ranges say green, with a forecast such as "red in N days". Ground control is a flight-surgeon screen where reports arrive only after the signal delay and the doctor's reply crosses the same delay back. Also: live space weather, cabin CO2, guided steps for yellow and red indicators, a Replay of the Day-143 scenario, a tab where anyone can drop their own resting-heart-rate CSV (it never leaves the browser), reaction and near-vision checks, Arabic advice, read-aloud and offline use.

HOW IT WORKS. An ASP.NET Core 8 server with SQLite validates and stores readings and pushes them live over SignalR to a React + Vite web app that is installable and works offline. The anomaly model (personal baseline, z-score) runs in C# and is checked against its Python reference by automated tests. The pulse comes from the phone camera through the fingertip (photoplethysmography in the browser), so it needs no extra hardware.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT. The crew learns of a drift days before fixed ranges would show it, knows what to do while Earth is minutes away, and sends Earth a report that says what was already tried. The same idea suits any isolated place where a doctor is far away.

WORKING FEATURES AND EVIDENCE. The app is live and usable. The camera pulse is a real measurement; it was checked on 53 real recorded signals (public BIDMC dataset) with 1.1 bpm mean error. Space weather is live from NOAA and NASA DONKI. A Monte Carlo virtual crew trial (hypotheses written before the run; settings chosen on one set, results on another) shows the calibrated personal baseline catching 97% of simulated drifts at 4.7% false alarms. Our first model false-alarmed on 94% of healthy crews, so we recalibrated it, and one pre-registered hypothesis failed and is reported in the app. 15 web test suites and 29 API tests run in CI.

LIMITATIONS. All crew data is synthetic and labeled; there are no real astronauts or patients. Oxygen and skin temperature are simulated in the app; blood pressure, glucose, sleep and mood are typed in. Camera pulse is approximate (a few bpm). The optional ESP32 hardware prototype (MAX30100 and DHT11) is hobby-grade and was not compared with a reference device. This is a prototype, not a medical device.

FUTURE PLANS. Test the baseline model on real wearable data with consent, review thresholds with clinicians, validate a wearable against a reference device, and add real oxygen and temperature sensing.

TOOLS. C#, ASP.NET Core 8, Entity Framework Core, SQLite, SignalR, JavaScript, React, Vite, Python, GitHub Actions, Microsoft Azure.
